title: Identifying Potential Protein Targets of BET Inhibitors in Enhancing Protein Folding
abstract: As life expectancy increases, humans face considerable health problems due to risk factors for neurodegenerative diseases such as Alzheimer’s and Parkinson’s Diseases. These diseases are associated with an accumulation of protein aggregation in neuronal cells due to protein misfolding and a subsequent decline in quality control. A major cellular protective mechanism regulating protein folding is the heat shock response (HSR). During cellular stress, the transcription factor Heat Shock Factor 1 (HSF1) activates a stress response which induces the expression of chaperone proteins aiding in the refolding of misfolded proteins and alleviating protein aggregation. Previously, a small molecule screen was performed employing a human cell line expressing a metastable luciferase folding sensor that misfolds during heat stress. The screen identified several BET (Bromodomain and Extra-Terminal domain) inhibitors that enhanced protein folding. Among the BET protein family, three candidates are known to directly interact with the HSF1 pathway: BRD4; EP300; and GCN5. To understand the mechanism of BET inhibitors in protein folding, human HAP1 (near-haploid) knock out (KO) cell lines of EP300, BRD4, or GCN5 containing a metastable luciferase folding sensor were used to quantify protein folding by luciferase assay. The results show reduced luciferase folding in the BRD4 and EP300 KO cell lines indicating they are regulated by HSF1. Identifying the target will allow for the design of higher potency and specificity of the small molecules to enhance protein folding, providing mechanistic insight into future therapeutics for treating neurodegenerative diseases.
